issues.description: The UML in the problem statement declares the attribute 'numberOfTutors' as type int, but the solution implementation declares the field as type short. This discrepancy between the specification and the provided solution can confuse students about the expected attribute type and may lead to inconsistent constructor/setter signatures or test mismatches.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the UML by declaring numberOfTutors as int (replace 'short numberOfTutors' with 'int numberOfTutors') and update any related code (constructor parameter, setter parameter, and usages) to use int. Ensure the template instructions and tests all refer to the same int type.

issues.description: The problem UML specifies numberOfTutors as an int and students will implement the constructor accordingly, but the solution's constructor signature takes a short for numberOfTutors. This mismatch between the expected constructor parameter type and the solution implementation can confuse students implementing the constructor to match the UML and tests.
issues.suggestedFix: Change the constructor parameter type for numberOfTutors to int in the solution (and in any example code). Update the constructor body accordingly so that it assigns an int parameter to the (int) field declared for numberOfTutors.

issues.description: The problem expects setters for all attributes (per the UML, numberOfTutors is an int), but the solution's setNumberOfTutors method accepts a short parameter. This creates an inconsistency between the expected setter signature students will implement and the solution's implementation.
issues.suggestedFix: Update the solution's setter signature to accept an int parameter (public void setNumberOfTutors(int numberOfTutors)) and adjust the implementation to assign the int parameter to the (int) field. Ensure the template and any example usage reflect the same signature.
